title: Template Method Pattern
oneLiner: Locks the overall steps of an algorithm in a base class, while letting subclasses customize individual steps.

hero.name: The Blueprint
hero.catchphrase: I set the steps. You fill in the details.
hero.power: Fixes an algorithm's overall sequence in one place, while individual steps stay overridable by subclasses.
hero.weakness: Leans on inheritance, so a step written for one report can't be reused by an unrelated class that isn't part of the same hierarchy.
hero.origin: The Blueprint appeared after three report generators — CSV, PDF, HTML — each duplicated the exact same 'fetch data, validate, sort, then export' sequence, differing only in the export step.

story.problem: CsvReport, PdfReport, and HtmlReport each implement their own `generate()` method that fetches data, validates it, sorts it, then exports — identical except for the final export step.
story.solution: The Blueprint puts the fixed sequence in an abstract base class's `generate()` method, calling `fetchData()`, `validate()`, `sort()`, then the abstract `export()` — which each subclass only needs to implement once.
story.result: The four-step sequence is defined exactly once. Each report subclass only writes the one step that's actually different: its export format.

before: Three report classes duplicate the same four-step sequence
A bug in step ordering has to be fixed in three places
Every new report format re-implements fetch/validate/sort from scratch
after: The four-step sequence is defined exactly once, in the base class
A bug fix in the sequence applies to every report automatically
A new report format only implements its one unique export step

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: Three report classes each contain a near-identical generate() method, differing only in the last step.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: I just found a sorting bug that exists in all three report classes, because they all copy-pasted the same broken sort call.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Blueprint rolls out a single master plan with four labeled steps, one still blank.
panels.speaker: The Blueprint
panels.dialogue: Stop copying the whole sequence. Define it ONCE — then let each report fill in only the step that's actually different.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: Report.generate() calls fetchData(), validate(), sort(), then the abstract export(). Subclasses only override export().
panels.speaker: The Blueprint
panels.dialogue: The sequence is locked here, in one place. You only write the one step that makes your report format unique.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The sorting bug fix happens in one file. All three report formats are fixed instantly.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: One fix, in one place, and every report format got it automatically. That bug can't come back in just one of them again.

useWhen: Several classes share the same overall algorithm structure but differ in one or two specific steps.
You want to enforce a consistent sequence of operations across all subclasses.
You want to let subclasses hook into specific points of an algorithm without letting them alter the sequence itself.
avoidWhen: The algorithm's steps need to be reusable outside this specific class hierarchy — Template Method locks you into inheritance.
There's only one variant of the algorithm — there's nothing to templatize yet.
The steps need to be reordered or skipped dynamically at runtime — composition-based approaches (like Strategy) are more flexible.
commonMistakes: Making too many steps overridable, so subclasses can effectively rewrite the whole algorithm anyway — defeating the point of a fixed sequence.
Using Template Method where a composed Strategy would be more flexible, since inheritance locks the relationship at compile time.
Forgetting to mark the template method itself `final`/non-overridable (where the language allows it), letting a subclass break the sequence entirely.
Not documenting which steps are required overrides versus optional hooks, confusing subclass authors.
explanation.realWorldExample: Test framework lifecycle methods (`setUp()` → `test()` → `tearDown()`, fixed order, customizable steps), data-import pipelines (fetch → validate → transform → load), and UI framework lifecycle hooks (`componentDidMount`-style sequences) are all Template Method.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: How is this different from Strategy? Both let you customize behavior.

conversation.speaker: The Blueprint
conversation.message: Strategy swaps a WHOLE algorithm via composition. I fix the overall SEQUENCE in a base class and only let subclasses customize specific STEPS within it — inheritance, not composition.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: When does that inheritance requirement bite me?

conversation.speaker: The Blueprint
conversation.message: When a step needs to be reused somewhere OUTSIDE this class hierarchy. Inheritance ties that step to me forever. If reuse across hierarchies matters, composition-based patterns serve you better.

codeBattle.scenario: Your data pipeline has three importers (CSV, JSON, XML) that each must fetch, validate, transform, and load data in that exact order — but the fetch/validate/load steps are identical across all three; only transform differs.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Blueprint locks the fetch/validate/transform/load sequence in one base class, letting each importer override only the transform step that actually differs.

quiz.question: What does the 'template method' itself typically do?
options: Defines the fixed sequence of steps, calling both concrete and overridable methods in order
Implements every step of the algorithm directly, with no overriding allowed
Is always abstract and left entirely to subclasses
Runs asynchronously in a separate thread from the rest of the algorithm
quiz.answer: Defines the fixed sequence of steps, calling both concrete and overridable methods in order
quiz.explanation: The template method is the orchestrator — it owns the sequence while delegating specific steps to (possibly overridden) methods.

quiz.question: What's the main risk of making too many steps overridable?
options: Subclasses can effectively rewrite the entire algorithm, defeating the purpose of a fixed sequence
The code becomes impossible to compile
The base class stops being reusable at all
It becomes impossible to write any subclasses
quiz.answer: Subclasses can effectively rewrite the entire algorithm, defeating the purpose of a fixed sequence
quiz.explanation: Template Method's value comes from guaranteeing a consistent sequence — over-exposing hooks erodes that guarantee.

quiz.question: What's a key limitation of Template Method compared to Strategy?
options: It relies on inheritance, so a step can't easily be reused by classes outside that specific hierarchy
It cannot customize any part of an algorithm
It can only be used with exactly two subclasses
quiz.answer: It relies on inheritance, so a step can't easily be reused by classes outside that specific hierarchy
quiz.explanation: Strategy's composition-based approach allows reusing an algorithm variant anywhere; Template Method's inheritance ties it to one hierarchy.

quiz.question: What's a classic real-world example of Template Method?
options: A test framework's fixed setUp → test → tearDown lifecycle, with each step customizable per test
quiz.answer: A test framework's fixed setUp → test → tearDown lifecycle, with each step customizable per test
quiz.explanation: Test lifecycles are a textbook Template Method: fixed order, customizable individual steps.
